text: Lesson 27 introduced RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE as the signal that memory grants are contended. Here's the deeper picture — what a grant actually is, how to see what's been handed out, and the real root cause behind most grant problems.

Sorts, hash joins, and hash aggregates need a memory workspace before they can even start executing, and SQL Server reserves that grant based on the optimizer's estimated row count and row width. That's an estimate, not a measurement — the seed of most of what goes wrong.

sys.dm_exec_query_memory_grants shows requested, granted, and actually used memory. A null grant_time with a populated request_time is a query still waiting — RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE made visible at the query level. A big gap between granted and max_used is the signature of an overestimated grant.

The grant pool is a finite, shared budget, so RESOURCE_SEMAPHORE waits happen even on a server with plenty of RAM if too many large grants are requested at once. The usual root cause isn't that queries need too much memory — it's a bad cardinality estimate, from stale statistics or parameter sniffing, requesting far more than the query will ever use.

Fix the estimate — update statistics, address parameter sniffing, rewrite the query — rather than just adding server memory, which treats the symptom and leaves the estimate wrong. Next up: the buffer pool's own health metric, and what actually moves it.
